claims.claim: Riggs reports that Carroll's main thrust is that Martin uses an argument from authenticity to justify his treatment of women, violence and non-Westerosi characters.
claims.source: Don Riggs, book review, Fafnir 6.2 (2019), reporting Shiloh Carroll

claims.claim: Riggs reports that Carroll sees Martin taking up medieval romance tropes only to subvert them by curtailing the reader's expectation with real-life intrusions.
claims.source: Don Riggs, book review, Fafnir 6.2 (2019), reporting Shiloh Carroll
claims.page: review body, on the chapter 'Romance and Anti-Romance'

claims.claim: Riggs quotes Carroll's closing judgement that in reaching for realism Martin created compelling characters, complex plots and subplots, and a masterpiece of worldbuilding.
claims.source: Shiloh Carroll, quoted at p.182 in Don Riggs's review, Fafnir 6.2 (2019)
claims.quote: Martin has created compelling characters, complex plots and subplots

claims.claim: Carroll characterises Martin's way of reimagining the Middle Ages as violent, dark, brutal, and relentlessly masculine.
claims.quote: violent, dark, brutal, and relentlessly masculine
claims.page: section 'Fantasy for People Who Hate Fantasy'

claims.claim: Carroll argues Martin goes too far in counteracting a rosy vision of the past with one covered in mud.
claims.quote: counteracting a rosy vision of the past with one covered in mud
claims.page: section 'Fantasy for People Who Hate Fantasy'

claims.claim: Carroll quotes Martin's defence that it is fundamentally dishonest to write a war story and leave rape out.
claims.source: George R. R. Martin, quoted by Shiloh Carroll, The Public Medievalist (2018)
claims.quote: if you write a war story and you leave that out
claims.page: section 'A Savage Beast in Every Man'

claims.claim: Mendlesohn writes that the immersive fantasy depends for its effectiveness on an assumption of realism that denies the need for explication.
claims.source: Farah Mendlesohn, Rhetorics of Fantasy (2008), Introduction
claims.quote: an assumption of realism that denies the need for explication

claims.claim: Mendlesohn writes that in immersive fantasy the reader has access to the protagonist's eyes and ears but is not provided with an explanatory narrative.
claims.source: Farah Mendlesohn, Rhetorics of Fantasy (2008), Introduction
claims.quote: we are not provided with an explanatory narrative

claims.feature: other: expository pressure of the chosen rhetoric
claims.claim: Mendlesohn writes that the quest fantasy's transitional narrative forces the author to describe and explain what the point of view character sees.
claims.source: Farah Mendlesohn, Rhetorics of Fantasy (2008), Introduction
claims.quote: forcing the author to describe and explain what
claims.page: Introduction, on quest and portal fantasy

claims.claim: Mendlesohn characterises the portal fantasy's language as the elaboration of the anthropologist, intensely descriptive and exploratory rather than assumptive.
claims.source: Farah Mendlesohn, Rhetorics of Fantasy (2008), Introduction
claims.quote: intensely descriptive and exploratory rather than assumptive

claims.claim: Mendlesohn writes that in portal fantasy the protagonist provides the reader with a guided tour of the landscapes.
claims.source: Farah Mendlesohn, Rhetorics of Fantasy (2008), Introduction
claims.quote: provides us with a guided tour of the landscapes

claims.claim: Mendlesohn writes that the point of view character of an immersive fantasy must take for granted the fantastic elements surrounding him or her.
claims.source: Farah Mendlesohn, Rhetorics of Fantasy (2008), Introduction
claims.quote: must take for granted the fantastic elements

claims.claim: Mendlesohn writes that successful immersive fantasy consciously negates the sense of wonder in favour of an atmosphere of ennui.
claims.source: Farah Mendlesohn, Rhetorics of Fantasy (2008), Introduction
claims.quote: consciously negates the sense of wonder
